messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Claire Morgan is a 35-year-old actor who came to treatment months after witnessing a violent assault outside a downtown train station in Los Angeles. She had been leaving an evening rehearsal when two uniformed transit officers confronted a young man on the platform. What began as shouting turned chaotic in seconds: one officer drew his weapon, people scattered, and the young man was forced to the ground while Claire stood frozen a few feet away, hearing him cry out and seeing the officer’s gun inches from his face. Even now, what comes back to her is not a smooth story but flashes—the dark blue uniform, the metallic glint of the weapon, one hand pressed into concrete, the sound of screaming, her own breath stopping. She says she cannot really “tell it right”; when she tries, the memory breaks apart into disconnected pieces, and at times it does not feel like remembering at all but like being dropped back into the platform as if it is happening again.

In the first weeks afterward, Claire became preoccupied with the fact that nothing seemed to happen to the officers involved. She followed the story online, waiting for charges or public outrage, and when neither came in the way she expected, she had come to believe that people with power could terrify someone in plain sight and face no consequences. That conclusion altered more than her opinion of the incident. It left her certain that reassurance about safety was basically meaningless, because if something so blatant could happen publicly and still go unanswered, then danger could appear anywhere and no one would really protect her. She also began to feel set apart from other people, especially castmates who talked easily about auditions, dating, and weekend plans. Their lives seemed to move along an ordinary track that she no longer occupied; she felt like an outsider who had seen something others either could not understand or could afford to ignore.

Those beliefs shaped what she did next. Claire stopped taking public transport entirely, even when it complicated travel to auditions and late rehearsals. On set or in acting class, she scanned the room and chose seats nearest exits or walls, somewhere she felt less exposed. If she spotted police or security uniforms on the street, or even prop weapons in a rehearsal context, she would leave, detour, or shut down internally until she could get away. She also found herself spending impulsively after especially hard days—ordering expensive clothes online, buying makeup she did not need, telling herself the packages gave her something else to focus on for a few hours. In her mind these choices were not irrational; if the world was fundamentally unsafe and other people could not really understand her position in it, then keeping distance and finding immediate comfort felt necessary.

But the strategies narrowed her life and seemed to confirm the very conclusions that had driven them. Avoiding the subway made her late for work and forced her into costly rideshares, which increased the shame she already felt about her spending. Turning down auditions because they were near transit hubs, or because uniformed officers might be present for crowd control, left her more cut off from colleagues and more convinced that she no longer belonged in the ordinary world. Each retreat seemed to deepen her sense of isolation. She would watch friends gather after rehearsals and head home alone, feeling that she had become someone separate, defined by vigilance and escape.

The memory itself remained raw and disorganized, and that quality fed her fear. Because the event returned in sensory fragments rather than a coherent account, Claire never felt it was over and placed in the past. A glimpse of a holstered weapon on a police officer at a coffee shop, the sight of a transit uniform near a studio, even the particular fluorescent light and echo of a station entrance could make her body react as though the assault were unfolding again. Once that surge hit—fear, horror, anger all at once—she became even more certain that safety was impossible to trust. And when she was already tense and scanning for threat, the fragments came more easily, intrusive and wordless, which only strengthened her conviction that the incident had changed her permanently and that no one who had not stood there could really understand.

Over time the loop tightened. The more she felt endangered, the more she watched for exits and avoided places where uniforms or weapons might appear; the more she lived that way, the more alone and different she felt. The more alone she felt, the more fixed became her belief that there had been no accountability and that she had been left carrying something society had simply absorbed and moved past. She finally sought help after leaving an important audition when she noticed an off-duty officer in the lobby and then spending nearly a week’s pay online that night, trying to calm herself. What frightened her most was not only the memories themselves but the possibility that this was her life now—that she would remain permanently outside other people’s safety, unable to work freely in the city she had built her career in. What she hopes, cautiously, is to be able to tell the story in words, sit in a room without calculating escape, and believe, even briefly, that the danger is not happening right now.
